utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Raseta, the Bench takes this opportunity to remind you that you are still bound by the declaration you made yesterday to tell the truth, nothing else but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I start with -- or resume my cross-examination, I would like to give a copy of the statement the witness gave to the ICTY investigators, and I would kindly ask the usher's assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we rely on your estimate last night that you won't be more than 10 minutes, Mr. Perovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that I shall finish within 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Raseta, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday the Prosecutor gave you a document, which is Prosecution exhibit number 95, the report you sent to the chief of the security administration of the VJ, General Dimitrijevic; do you recall that? That's the report dated 2nd May.

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which page are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the document in general now, but I'm actually dealing with page 22 of your statement, paragraph 72. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: This is a document you confirmed in your response to the Prosecutor that you drafted it and sent it to General Dimitrijevic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but on the basis of the contents produced by the security organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: I have two questions in relation to this document. First is the following: In paragraph 71 of your statement to the OTP, you state that you have no knowledge of any attacks, especially not air attacks, on the refugees in Western Slavonia during the so-called Operation Flash. However, in this report you state on page 1, the last paragraph of -- on that page, and I'm referring to the report for General Dimitrijevic, that during combat activities on the 1st of May, 1995, two, as you put it, Ustasha MiG-21 aircraft were struck down. That's what you state in your report to General Dimitrijevic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that this is contained in the report. However, I repeat again that this is the part of the report drafted by the security organ that I merely took over. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: I do understand. However, as far as I understand, you sent unverified information to General Dimitrijevic in the security administration of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's also the report of Commander Perovic, which was sent along the relevant lines to the VJ General Staff. If my part of the report was incorrect, so was that part of the report too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic, you actually start asking the next question before the interpreter is finished. Could you slow down, please? You're moving very fast. And, Mr. Raseta, you also reply very quickly. Can you take a break after the question, just to allow the interpreters to interpret. I could hear the interpreter speaking without a breath in between. I think we shouldn't subject them to so much pressure. Thank you very much, Mr. Perovic. Take it slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: On page 3 of this report you sent to General Dimitrijevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise for the interjection. Could we perhaps see this report on the e-court because I think it's very difficult for the witness to answer questions about what's in the report without seeing the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May we see the report on the e-court, please, Mr. Perovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's Exhibit 95, which was presented to the witness by the OTP yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's true. Let's have it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: We're referring to page 3 of the report, that's to say the last page, and the paragraph wherein you state that there was a discussion at the meeting of the Supreme Defence Council of the RSK, I will read this paragraph out to you. The report reads: "All the participants in the discussion and proposals agreed that Ustashas should not be given in to. However, the approaches as to the method whereby the situation should be resolved differed all except for Martic, Celeketic and some other closest associates of the Main Staff were in favour of a peaceful solution of the newly arisen situation by way of negotiations, and as a pre-condition for that, they require that the commander of the 18th Corps of the army of the RSK should sign a cease-fire agreement with the commander of the other warring party, which would mean a surrender and a capitulation of this part of the territory." My question in connection with this is as follows: Were all those present at the meeting of the Supreme Council in favour -- except for Martic and Celeketic, as you put it, in favour of the idea that a part of the RSK territory, namely Western Slavonia, should be the subject of a capitulation.

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: All those present, except for Martic and Celeketic, were in favour of a capitulation in Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Another question in this context. Do you know that under the RSK constitution capitulation is provided for as one of the gravest crimes?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that. I read the constitution, but I don't recall that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions in relation to this document. In your statement for the OTP you state, among other things, that on the basis of your military knowledge and experience, you did not deem the use of the Orkan, VBR Orkan, to have been an appropriate weapon to be used against Zagreb in retaliation for Western Slavonia. You also state that on this occasion innocent people were casualties. And in view of the fact that a good part of your career you spent in armoured and mechanised units, as you state in your personal background, my question is the following: On the basis of your experience, on your relevant experience, what would have been an adequate response to such a situation, since you concluded that the course taken was inadequate?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The appropriate course of action would have been to fire at targets from which the territory of the Republic of Serbian Krajina was fired upon. I'm primarily referring to targeting targets that are points, whereas I said yesterday that the multiple-barrelled rocket launcher aims at an area and one never knows how large an area will be hit. Artillery pieces are one type of weaponry, and multiple-barrel rocket launchers are quite another.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In connection with this, or, rather, with your remark that innocent people were killed when Zagreb was shelled, I have the following question for you: Do you know how people were killed in Western Slavonia during Operation Flash?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 100 people. I believe so. Of course, I'm not trying to find any justification for that either. I believe, and I do not approve of -- of the suffering and the killing of innocent people on either side.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: According to Croatian sources we were able to hear about, 168 people were killed in Operation Flash. Do you know how many people were killed in the shelling of Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the figures are at around 30 and about 100 wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: According to Croatian sources that we arrived at during this trial, there were five killed persons as a result of the shelling of Zagreb. Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday at one point in your testimony you mentioned retaliation. That's how you called or styled the shelling of Zagreb. I'm asking you as a military expert why did you use that particular term?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sorry for the interruption. I would just clarify that this witness, while he does have a military background, has not been offered, certainly by the Prosecution, I don't believe his expertise as a military expert has been established as such. And consequently I don't have any objection to him answering the question, but I don't think it should be presented as expert opinion under the Rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you hear that, Mr. Perovic? Do you have any response?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I accept the remark by my learned friend, and I will rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: I will omit the part of the question referring to him as a military expert, but the rest of my question stands.

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't I who used the term "retaliation," rather, it was General Celeketic. I said yesterday that retaliation was not a term normally used during the military studies.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: How would you then qualify the shelling of Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The return fire and revenge for what had happened in Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: As revenge or as an attempt to put a stop to the attack against Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was far too late to stop the attack against Western Slavonia. By that time the Croatian forces had captured almost the entire territory of Western Slavonia. And I'm saying by the time Zagreb was shelled, at least I believe so. You seem to be saying that this particular action was taken at the -- in the initial stage of the attack against Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In your report to General Dimitrijevic you state that five to 6.000 people, refugees in Western Slavonia, of whom more than 3.000 were elderly and children, were encircled by the Croatian forces and even subject of strikes and that this was happening between the 1st and the 3rd of May, 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. However, I repeat this was not my data, but rather the data received from the intelligence department.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Let us move on to a different topic, which indirectly is related to the former topic. At the meeting of the Supreme Defence Council of the RSK, you came to know that General Celeketic, the commander of the Main Staff of the army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, gave his resignation after the shelling of Zagreb. What was the reason for his removal or, rather, for his resignation?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told those of us who were present that he could not ever forgive himself for having lost Western Slavonia when he had promised the president of the Republic that not even an inch of the land would be captured whilst he was commander. I believe this to have been the main reason for his resignation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 76 on page 24 of your statement for the OTP, you mention as the reason for his resignation something quite different. You state that the Celeketic had told you that the chief of the VJ General Staff, Colonel General Perisic decided to fire him and replace him with General Mrksic. Is that the correct quotation from your statement?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The quotation is correct. However, what you're asking me about now is something that I arrived at as a result of what General Celeketic told me himself. I believe that the information concerning Perisic wanting to fire him was something that reached us only after Celeketic had resigned.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: If that's true, then I am going to ask you the following: The withdrawal of Celeketic or his removal, for which even Belgrade was designated as the place where the initiative was launched for, could it be perceived as a punishment for the shelling of Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot categorically claim either way, because I do not have any information to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: I asked you this because in the following paragraph, that's to say paragraph 77, you state that from the chief of the intelligence service of the RSK, Knezevic, you learnt that the big boss, and I suppose you meant Milosevic, was very angry at the -- with the shelling of Zagreb. Did you have any such information?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, except for what Lieutenant-Colonel Knezevic told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Did Knezevic tell you anything else in addition to the fact that the big boss was very angry? Did the big boss mention a dangerous escalation of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: That's contained in your report to Dimitrijevic.

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please refer me to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, not in your report to Dimitrijevic, but rather in your statement for the OTP. "Knezevic told me that the 'big boss' considered the shelling of Zagreb a dangerous escalation ..."

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Is that how Knezevic put it to you?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You spoke, among other things, of the fact that Colonel Gacic refused to carry out Celeketic's order to shell Sisak. This is contained in paragraph 82 of your statement on page 26. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: After all these events Gacic went back to the army of Yugoslavia, and as you put it, he was not punished for having refused to carry out Celeketic's order; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Does this not illustrate that the VJ and the SVK were not, after all, one tissue, as you described it yesterday?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: However, Gacic refused to carry out an order in the SVK and not in the army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. For having done that, he should have incurred consequences down here and not up there in the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, in the VJ there were no consequences for him, were there?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 90 on page 28 of your report -- of your statement you state that while you -- that during your service in the security organs of the SVK, you did not see any reports on alleged violations of customs and laws of war. My question is the following: Was this the case because there were none, or were there some other reasons?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In stating this I referred primarily to the documentation that I had at my disposal in the Security Service, that's to say, that I did not come across any such documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In this same paragraph you also state the following: "I don't recall that murder or other crimes were widespread, but there were isolated cases of murder." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: That's an accurate piece of information?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 91 you state that in 1994 a military prosecutor office was established in the SVK. You go on to say the president of the military court was Colonel Milan Vignjevic. Did you file before this Prosecutor's office any report which had to do with alleged crimes?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. If there were such instances, then such reports must have been filed by the police, by the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: But nobody placed any obstacles in your way of cooperating with that particular institution?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions for you, Mr. Raseta.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have completed my cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Perovic. Mr. Black?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Black. Judge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Judge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Raseta, I am going ask you a few questions and we can get done with this. Let's start at the end where you've just been testifying, while it is fresh. You have been asked a question about what you said in paragraph 90 of your report where you state that there were isolated killings, and you further state that you do not recall these being investigated. You remember what has just been asked? You remember that, Mr. Raseta?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Raseta.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Raseta, your microphone is not on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this related for the most part to individual killings that occurred in the units of our army, whether by accident or because of quarrels among the men. It was those killings that I was referring to, not other kinds of killings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, I understand that. I hadn't asked my question yet. My question really to you is: Are such isolated killings normally investigated in the military?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, an investigation is obligatory, it's mandatory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And you also testified this afternoon that the shelling of Zagreb was too late to stop the attack on Western Slavonia. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just for the record, when was Western Slavonia attacked?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the precise date and time, but I do know that all these events, which occurred in Western Slavonia, the withdrawal of the 18th Corps and parts of the population, most of the population, had already occurred. They had already reached the borders of Republika Srpska. Practically Western Slavonia was just about to fall or had already been taken by the Croatian forces. And Zagreb was fired upon on the second day, I think, or I don't know what day, but later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The second day after what? The second day after the fall of Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When Western Slavonia was already controlled by the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You testified yesterday to the effect that the Yugoslav army gave the SVK logistical support. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you able to flush out for us what you actually mean by logistical support? Can we give specific kinds of support that were given by the VJ to the SVK?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was exclusively logistical support, meaning fuel, lubricating oil, ammunition, foodstuffs, quartermaster supplies, weapons. I'm referring to artillery weapons. That was what logistical support meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Excuse my ignorance of military affairs. What is meant by quartermaster supplies?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Footwear and clothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yesterday you mentioned that the shelling of Zagreb would have been -- reporting of the shelling of Zagreb would have been made to Mr. Milan Martic. This was in answer to a question whether you knew that whether he was aware of the shelling. Do you remember that statement?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm certain that he knew that General Celeketic, the commander, would have had to inform him of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you aware of any disciplinary action taken by Mr. Martic against those who shelled Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You also mentioned yesterday that the attack on Zagreb was not mentioned in the meeting of the 1st of May, 1995. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Was such an attack mentioned at any other meeting before it took place?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Captain Raseta, I have no further questions. Mr. Black, any questions arising from the questions by the Court?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: None, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Perovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only one, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: With respect to the questions put by His Honour, as for the length of Operation Flash, the combat operation in Western Slavonia, are you aware of when an agreement was reached with the Croatian government with the mediation of Mr. Akashi and UNPROFOR in Western Slavonia, do you know anything about this agreement?

utterances.speaker: RADE RASETA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Perovic. Mr. Raseta, thank you so much for coming to testify. This is the end of your testimony. You are now excused. You may stand down. And thank you once again for coming to testify.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And good day to you all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we call the next witness, there are just a few housekeeping matters to raise with the parties. The Prosecution filed a motion for protective measures for Witness MM-088. I think this motion was filed on the 28th of April. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, I think it's Witness 080.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And I believe that this witness is coming immediately after the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We would anticipate that he would testify -- he won't testify this week, it will be no sooner than Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. The reason the Chamber raises this point is because it does seem as if he has to come fairly soon, Mr. Milovancevic, and the Chamber is mindful of the fact that the Defence has not had the full two weeks within which to respond. Nonetheless, in view of the scheduling of the witness, the Chamber would like to know whether the Defence is in a position to respond as quickly as possible to this motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we received the submission on the 28th of April, and we can give our written response tomorrow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The Chamber is grateful to you for that accommodation, and the Chamber would like to repeat its request to the Prosecution. The request was first made on the 8th of March, to try and make these motions timelinessly [sic] to allow the Defence to answer in time. Don't want to belabour the point, but just want to repeat that request. And with respect to this witness this request is even strengthened by the fact that the witness, according to the statement expressed concern as early as October 2005 about his fears to testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I certainly take the Court's point. With respect to this witness, I will only say this: That the -- that the fears that were expressed at that time were -- were vague and it was not in the context of this witness testifying. At that point you will recall that the witness was not even on the witness list of the Prosecution. He was added only later. And it -- the motion that was just filed was as a result of a conversation with the witness that occurred very recently. But, having said that, I take the Court's point. We'll try to file these as quickly as possible when we get the information. Oftentimes we get that information in the process of scheduling the witness which occurs only a week or two before the witness appears, so that's why these motions have come this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand. The discussion that you refer to as "recent," it's as recently as February of this year; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I can't speak with certainty on that, but I believe that it's not February, I believe it's within the past couple of weeks. But I could be corrected on that. I may be wrong about that, but that's my recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We shall not belabour the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Once again, thank you, Mr. Milovancevic, if you can file that response tomorrow. There was sometime back some discussion about the agreed facts. The Bench is mindful of the fact that at some stage it was agreed that there was no need to file any corrected version of those agreed facts. But it's been brought to the attention of the Chamber that without the corrected version filed as an exhibit, this does -- it's -- those facts are sort of floating and if they could perhaps be filed as an exhibit, and given an exhibit number, that would be much helpful. I'm sorry that the Bench is causing you a duplication of work, but it's all questions of procedure that we're still grappling with.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour it will no difficulty to do that. I'll undertake with the Defence to coordinate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That would be much appreciated. Thank you very much. Could we move into private session for the next item, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, unfortunately I have to inform the Court that we have a little gap here in the schedule. We had anticipated that this last witness would go longer and that he would take two days, a day for the direct examination and then a full day for the cross-examination; however, he went more quickly than we anticipated. So our next witness actually will not be ready until tomorrow at 2.15 and I really apologise for that. However, there are a few housekeeping matters of our own that I would like to raise, if I may. But before I do that, Mr. Black wanted me to ask if he could be excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Black, you are excused from hearing about the housekeeping matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, and I told Defence counsel yesterday that I would raise these matters, so it is no surprise. But what I thought would be helpful would be -- as we're nearing the end of the Prosecution case, if we would anticipate perhaps the schedule that would occur between the Prosecution case and the Defence case, and I thought it would be useful to do that now in advance so that everybody would be prepared for whatever schedule is decided upon by the Trial Chamber. We -- on our current schedule, we anticipate that the Prosecution case will finish by the 2nd of June of this year. Of course there may be slippage, but I wouldn't anticipate that it would be more than a few days or a week. So assume that we finish the 2nd of June, which is in a month. What I thought would be helpful is to discuss briefly what occurs after that. Now, naturally under Rule 98 bis, the Defence may, if it chooses, make a submission that the Prosecution has not met its case on any or all counts. 98 bis, as the Court is no doubt aware, has been recently amended in the last year or so, so that is now -- what used to be a lengthy written process is now an oral process. The submissions are made by the Defence orally, the Prosecution responds orally, the Trial Chamber rules on that orally. What I would imagine, what I would propose, I should say, is that after the close of the Prosecution case that we set aside approximately a week for that process to occur. And the reason I say a week is that I would imagine the Defence would want perhaps a few days to prepare a 98 bis submission, prepare their oral submission, the -- they could then make that submission, the Prosecution could respond that day or perhaps would ask for the Court's indulgence to respond the next day. Simply if the Prosecution has to kind of marshal its evidence and make its response specifically. And then the Trial Chamber could rule on that within whatever time is appropriate. But that process could be -- could be completed, I would think, within a week or 10 days. After that I would propose that the Defence -- that the Defence be required to make its submissions under Rule 65 ter (G). That Rule requires the Defence at the close of the Prosecution case, and I would think after the 98 bis process has taken place, to file their witness list with their summaries of witness -- what the witnesses will testify about, their exhibit list and so forth, much as the Prosecution did at the beginning of its case. Once that is filed, I would propose that that be filed immediately after the 98 bis ruling by the Trial Chamber. Once that is filed, I would ask for -- that there be two weeks before the Defence case begins. Because the Prosecution needs, and I would submit is entitled to, that minimum amount of time in order to prepare for the testimony of the Defence witnesses. That process entails checking to see if we have any information about these witnesses, doing searches and so forth. And two weeks is really, I would submit, the kind of minimum amount of time that we need in order to do that. So on that schedule, what I'm imagining is approximately a three-week period between the end of the Prosecution case and the beginning of the Defence case, assuming that those suggested dates can be met. If we could move briefly into private session, just to address one point on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Before I raise that last matter, I would just say that with respect to the proposed schedule and Defence counsel's response, and I will -- I will discuss this with Defence counsel, and maybe we can reach some agreement, but of course the burden, there is a burden on the Defence here, because they -- they are the ones who have to produce the witness list and exhibit list and 65 ter list, so that is usually I can say frankly where delay occurs, and so that's why I want to raise it now so that maybe that could be avoided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I would imagine that the data for that kind of preparation is already available for the Defence. It's just a question of putting it down on paper and giving it to you. They already know what witnesses they are going to call, what summaries they intend to file. One would imagine.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: One would imagine. And if that's true, then I would agree with Your Honour that there would be no difficulty meeting the proposed dead-line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Looking at Mr. Milovancevic's face, it looks like indeed my imagination is correct. Am I right, Mr. Milovancevic? All right. The smile says it all. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, the last matter that I wanted to raise, and I've discussed this with the Defence, is the Court is perhaps aware of the -- of the summer recess that has been -- that we have this year, and it's -- it's a little odd because it's kind of early.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 17th July to 6th August.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Correct. And I have discussed this with the Defence, and I'm wondering if -- I mean, I raised it with the Defence, but I think I can make the proposal on behalf of the Prosecution and the Defence, is if we could, rather than resuming on the 7th of August, if we could resume one week later on the 14th of August. And that has to do with schedules of the Prosecution and of the Defence regarding personal obligations. And I know it's a loss of a week of trial time, I'm aware of that. I don't believe that at least speaking for the Prosecution, that we have asked for any time off from the schedule. Of course there have been gaps, I'm getting a look, I don't think we have. In any event, I -- it would be greatly appreciated, I can -- speaking for the Prosecution, and I think also for the Defence if we could extend it that -- an extra week. I do think that during that break time work will be done towards the trial. We won't just be taking a break, though we will obviously be doing that. There will be work being done with respect to the final briefs, with respect to other ongoing trials, so it's not completely lost time. And, as I said, all I can say is that I would be grateful if we could do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you say this is for personal obligations, personal reasons?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: For myself, yes, Your Honour. I would like to be quite candid about that. It is a family obligation back in the United States that I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And can the Chamber -- is it possible to slot that week in the break between the Prosecution case and the schedule we've been talking about, so that at least it is used productively in chambers rather than just sort of --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand, Your Honour. I'm not sure I understand what Your Honour is saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, we have just been talking about scheduling once the Prosecution case closes and what is going to happen, and I'm just saying, is it likely that that week that the Prosecution is asking for, can be part of the three-week break, or whatever length of time break that we have between the close of the Prosecution case and the opening of the Defence case?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You mean that we would shorten that three -- take one week from that three weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Be a part of that break. Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, if Your Honour -- and I'm sorry if I'm looking a little bit slow here, but if Your Honour is saying the break between the Prosecution and the Defence case may fall at that time, I don't think it will, but if Your Honour is saying that instead of a three-week break between Prosecution and Defence, we take a two-week break -- I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The first, the former. The Bench means the former.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I see. I don't think that will occur because -- no, no, I'm sorry. Your Honour, the time of that one week that is important, it is that week in August that is important. It's not flexible from my point of view. And I do think that the Defence also would appreciate that week. As Your Honour is aware, August is traditionally the time when people take holiday and take breaks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not aware, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, that's certainly true in Europe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I come from the south.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Right. And I come from -- I don't come from Europe myself, but I've grown accustomed in my years here. And in any event, all I can say, Your Honour, is that we would be grateful if we could have that week. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Milovancevic, is it correct that that week in August would suit the Defence also?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Your Honour. We have already discussed this matter with our learned friends from the Prosecution, and this is, in fact, a joint submission on our part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: To enjoy a traditional European holiday in that week. Thank you very much. Now I understand. The Chamber has heard you. Thank you very much. You are not asking for an answer now, are you? Or would you like to have it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's up to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Let me find out from Their Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. By a majority, your application has been granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I repeat that we are most grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Court adjourned until tomorrow at quarter past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 4th day of May, 2006, at 2.15 p.m. 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 3.22 p.m.,
